lookalikes.note: A true morel is one hollow space from top to bottom and its head is pitted with ridges. This is chambered inside and folded like a brain.

lookalikes.note: Cut it in half. The inside here is HARD and purple-black to purple-grey even when young; an edible puffball is pure white and soft. The rind is 1-3mm thick and tough, not paper thin.

hazard.note: Raw or undercooked morels upset many people. Never eaten raw.

taxa.note: Hollow from the top of the head to the bottom of the stem, in one continuous space. Cut it lengthwise and look: that is the test, and it is the only field character that settles this against a false morel.

lookalikes.note: A false morel is chambered or cottony inside, not one hollow space, and its head is folded like a brain rather than pitted with ridges.

hazard.note: Reported to disagree with more people than the yellow morel, particularly with alcohol. Never eaten raw.

taxa.note: Ridges darken toward black as it ages while the pits stay paler. Hollow throughout, like all true morels.

lookalikes.note: Chambered inside rather than hollow, and folded rather than pitted.

taxa.note: On conifer, and here that means high up — above about 5,000 feet. Thin, pure white, and without the substantial flesh of an oyster mushroom.

lookalikes.note: An oyster mushroom is on broadleaf wood and is thick and fleshy. This is on conifer, and it is thin. If the wood is not certain, do not resolve it in the field.

taxa.note: Pink gills that darken to chocolate, a brown spore print, and no sac at the base. Each of those alone separates it from a destroying angel, which keeps white gills, drops a white print, and stands in a bag.

lookalikes.note: A destroying angel keeps white gills at every age, drops a white print, and sits in a membranous sac. If the base was not dug up, that question is not answered.
